sentences: Settle in.
You're starting in Midtown, right in front of Grand Central Terminal — so take a second and just look up.
Start with the 42nd Street facade.

What crowns it is The Glory of Commerce, called America's greatest monumental sculpture — forty-eight feet of it, designed by the French sculptor Jules-Félix Coutan, carved across the river in Long Island City by Donnelly and Ricci, then hoisted up piece by piece in 1914.

At its center a wing-capped Mercury, Roman god of travel and commerce, throws his arms wide in welcome, while Hercules lounges beside him in a strangely placid pose and Minerva, ancient guardian of cities, gazes down on the mayhem of 42nd Street.
Its base is Connecticut Stony Creek granite, its upper stretch Indiana limestone.
And that clock beneath Mercury's foot is the largest single piece of Tiffany glass anywhere in the world.

The architects were thinking like Romans, who once framed the entrances to great cities with monumental arches meant to awe everyone passing through; they saw railroad terminals as exactly that kind of gateway and filled this one with the symbols of imperial Rome.
Ten colossal fluted Doric columns tower over Park Avenue to prove the point.

None of it was guaranteed — when the original Penn Station opened across town and threatened their railroad, the Vanderbilt dynasty tore down Cornelius Vanderbilt's 19th-century Grand Central Depot and rebuilt it as a 20th-century showpiece.
You'll find the old tycoon himself out front, a statue of Cornelius Vanderbilt beneath the great central window.
Two hundred buildings came down to make room, and when the doors opened on February 2, 1913, the bill ran to eighty million dollars.
What they got was beaux-arts — steel, granite and limestone — and still the most breathtaking building of its kind in New York.
Step into the Main Concourse and it hardly feels like somewhere you'd catch a train — more a glorious ballroom.
Terry Gilliam saw it too; the closing scene of his 1991 film The Fisher King turns this very floor into a ballroom of waltzing commuters.
That floor is Tennessee pink marble, an acre of it, with vintage ticket counters cut from Italian Bottocino marble.
Electric light was one of the station's proudest tricks, so bare bulbs still glow along the walls and across the massive chandeliers overhead.
Now look up — nine stories up — to a vaulted turquoise and gold-leaf sky, where the constellations of the zodiac shine out of 59 fiber-optic lights scattered among 2,500 painted stars.
Study it and you'll notice the eight constellations run backwards.
A mistake? Apparently not.
Its French designer, the painter Paul César Helleu, wanted the stars shown from God's point of view — from the outside looking in.

Moisture later forced a faithful repaint by Charles Gulbrandsen in 1944, and when the architects Beyer Blinder Belle restored the ceiling they left one small rectangular patch of soot in the northwest corner, beneath the crab, as a marker of how filthy it had become.
Before you leave, find the Whispering Gallery on the vaulted landing below the bridge that links the Concourse to Vanderbilt Hall.
Put a friend in the arched corner diagonally across from you and murmur something — it carries straight to their ear.

People propose here, a lot, and if the answer's yes, chilled champagne waits right through the door at the Grand Central Oyster Bar, under a tiled vaulted ceiling by the Catalan engineer Rafael Guastavino — with an elevator beside it climbing to a snootier old gem, the bar called The Campbell.
Leave Grand Central behind and head for the Chrysler Building, about five minutes on foot.
Walter P. Chrysler paid for this tower out of his own pocket, and he gave his architect, William Van Alen, one instruction — build me something higher than the Eiffel Tower.

Trouble was, the men behind the Bank of America wanted the exact same crown, so they hired Van Alen's former partner and sworn enemy, H. Craig Severance, to put up the world's tallest building down on Wall Street.
Severance finished first, at 927 feet, and figured he'd won.

Then Van Alen sprang the surprise he'd been assembling in secret inside the building — a 185-foot spire of seven radiating steel arches, hoisted up through a false roof and bolted in place in about ninety minutes.
That silver spike shot the Chrysler to 1,046 feet, a full 117 feet over Severance's tower — an unbeatable margin.
Severance, who'd been certain his own Wall Street skyscraper would top the world, was outraged; the spire, people said, was as much an act of vengeance as of engineering.
And yet the Chrysler wore the world's-tallest crown for barely a year before the Empire State Building snatched it away.
Still, this is art deco at its peak — the useful fused with the beautiful, and one of the finest examples ever built.

The style had taken its name only in 1925, at the Paris Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs, and its sunbursts, chevrons, and zigzags soon turned up on everything from jewelry to comic books to trains, remaking New York into a silvery science-fiction metropolis.
For the best view from the street, go to the corner of Lexington Avenue and 43rd Street and look straight up.
That scalloped crown sits on the tower like a jaunty jester's cap.
Steel American eagles crouch at the corners of the 61st floor, angular and gleaming, as if ready to leap.
Lower down, on the 31st floor, winged hubcaps echo the radiator caps of a 1929 Chrysler — the carmaker's signature carved in steel.
There's no restaurant or observation deck up top, but the lobby — once a Chrysler showroom — is a lavish consolation.
Amber light warms dark African wood and marble set against the brash steel of industrial America.
The elevators are the real jewels, their Egyptian lotus patterns inlaid with Japanese ash, Oriental walnut, and Cuban plum-pudding wood.
And overhead spreads Edward Trumbull's ceiling mural, Transport and Human Endeavor — said to be the world's largest — full of airplanes, buildings, and workers on Chrysler's assembly lines.
For the whole building at once, though, you'd have to cross town and look back from the deck of the very tower that beat it — the Empire State Building.
From Chrysler Building, carry on to New York Public Library, about a 13-minute walk away.
A few blocks back, you passed the Chrysler Building, where the architect William Van Alen secretly built a 200-foot spire inside the stairwell and hoisted it into place in just an hour and a half.
It shot the tower to 1,046 feet, 117 higher than his rival's, and the reveal left H. Craig Severance furious.
Two marble lions keep watch over the steps up from Fifth Avenue, and the story goes they roar whenever a virgin walks past.
A mayor gave them their names.
Fiorello LaGuardia called them Patience and Fortitude in the 1930s, after the two qualities he thought New Yorkers needed to survive the Great Depression.
The lions were designed by the sculptor Edward Clark Potter and carved by the Piccirilli brothers, a family of famous marble cutters.
Look up past them, and you're facing what many art historians call the finest Beaux Arts building in America.
Carrère and Hastings finished it in 1911 for more than nine million dollars, and when it was dedicated it was the largest marble structure ever raised in the United States.
For the front they borrowed from Paris — the twin palaces on the north side of the Place de la Concorde, the same French Renaissance style, a careful harmony of columns, pediments, and statuary.

This was New York's gilded age, when architects trained in France came home with European ideals: gleaming white limestone instead of brownstone, ground floors lifted for grand staircase entrances, Corinthian columns and sculptured keystones everywhere.
Officially it's the Stephen A. Schwarzman Building, the main branch of the New York Public Library, and it was named a National Historic Landmark in 1965.
Inside wait 8.7 million books and artifacts, along with one of the longest and most famous reading rooms in the world — the recently restored Rose Main Reading Room and its lavish coffered ceiling.
Writers like Norman Mailer and Alfred Kazin worked under that ceiling, and it's still open to anyone who's working — surely the most glamorous coworking space on earth.

Then there's the treasure in the Rare Book Division: a Gutenberg Bible printed around 1455, one of just 48 that survive from the roughly 180 that Johannes Gutenberg made after he invented the printing press around 1440.
When it arrived from Europe, the story goes, officials at the New York Customs House were made to remove their hats in honor of the holy book.
The library's had quite a cinematic life, too.
Ghostbusters opens right here in 1984, down in the haunted stacks, with those same marble lions and the Rose Main Reading Room on screen.
In Sex and the City, this is where Mr Big jilts Carrie in her Vivienne Westwood wedding dress in 2008.
And in The Thomas Crown Affair, the foyer sneakily stands in for the Metropolitan Museum of Art, where Pierce Brosnan's thieving playboy meets his match in Rene Russo's sultry detective.
This has always been a writer's town.
In the 19th century, Herman Melville, Edith Wharton, and Walt Whitman all congregated here.

And it only got livelier — the liquor-fueled literary salons of the poet-communist John Reed in the 1910s, the acid wisecracks of the Algonquin Round Table in the 1920s, and the thinly veiled novels of Dawn Powell in the '40s, skewering the city's media establishment.
From New York Public Library, make your way on to Bryant Park, about an 8-minute walk away.

That fountain up ahead? Diane Keaton stood right there, breathlessly debriefing her husband Woody Allen about the elderly neighbor she's convinced is a murderer — the opening beat of Manhattan Murder Mystery, 1993.
Allen packs the film with New York, so you also get the National Arts Club over in Gramercy Park.

Just behind the beaux-arts New York Public Library, this four-acre lawn is a genuine break from the crush of midtown, with benches, statuary, and shaded promenades of London planetrees that feel closer to the Tuileries in Paris than to anything you'd expect here.
Grab a coffee at one of the European-style kiosks, take a bench, and look up at the towers ringing the green.
On any decent day, something free is happening — juggling classes at noon, yoga, painting workshops, beginner Italian, even birding tours.
From May through October the Sixth Avenue end turns into a stage for Broadway performers and free concerts, and Monday nights bring open-air movies out on the lawn.
At the east edge you'll find one of the city's most popular outdoor bars.
A carousel turns nearby.
Until 2010, New York Fashion Week pitched up here twice a year, before it moved uptown to Lincoln Center.
Come winter, the lawn becomes The Pond — a free ice rink with lessons if you want them, wrapped by a European-style holiday market of gift booths and hot chocolate.
None of this hints at the ground's first act. Back in 1853, this same expanse hosted the Crystal Palace Fair.
And here's the part that's genuinely hard to square — through the 1970s, this leafy oasis was a crime-ridden hellscape, known simply as Needle Park.
Leaving Bryant Park behind, we head for Times Square — about a twelve-minute walk.
Before the lights hit, look back at the mile you've just walked.
At Grand Central, The Fisher King turned the Main Concourse into a ballroom of waltzing commuters.
At the Chrysler Building, William Van Alen hid a spire in an elevator shaft and raised it to 1,046 feet, beating his rival Severance by 117 feet.
At the library, two marble lions — Patience and Fortitude, named by Mayor LaGuardia in the 1930s — still keep watch.
And Bryant Park, a crime-ridden 'Needle Park' in the 1970s, is now where the city goes ice-skating.
The most famous square on earth started as a nobody — an unremarkable crossroads called Longacre Square.
What changed it was a deal between two ambitious men: August Belmont, building the city's first subway line from Lower Manhattan up to Harlem, and Adolph Ochs, publisher of the New York Times.

Belmont figured a Midtown business hub would fill his trains, so he pitched Ochs on moving the paper to Broadway and 42nd Street — an in-house station meant faster distribution and more sales to the flood of commuters.
Then he talked Mayor George B McClellan Jr into renaming the square for the broadsheet.
In the winter of 1904–05, both the subway station and the Times' new headquarters at One Times Square opened for business.
To celebrate, the Times threw a New Year's Eve party in 1904, firing fireworks off its rooftop.
By 1907 the square was so built up that those fireworks were ruled a hazard, and the paper needed a new crowd-puller.
The answer was a 700-pound wood-and-iron ball, lowered from the roof of One Times Square to welcome 1908.
Around a million people still crowd in every New Year's Eve to watch a Waterford crystal ball drop at midnight.
This is the New York of collective fantasies.

It's where Al Jolson 'makes it' in the 1927 film The Jazz Singer, where Alfred Eisenstaedt caught a sailor kissing a nurse on V-J Day in 1945, and where Alicia Keys and Jay-Z sang about the concrete jungle.
But the theater got here first.
The neighborhood's first playhouse was the Empire, opened in 1893 on Broadway between 40th and 41st.
Two years later a cigar manufacturer and part-time comedy writer named Oscar Hammerstein opened the Olympia, then in 1900 the Republic — today the children's theater New Victory.
That set off a run of new venues, including the New Amsterdam and the Lyceum, both still going.
Those early houses grew straight out of vaudeville, staging popular plays and suggestive comedies.

By the 1920s they'd swelled into full spectacles — lighthearted musicals like Show Boat, Hammerstein's epic about performers on a Mississippi steamboat, spinning off classics like Cole Porter's 'Let's Misbehave.'
But the district was also becoming a launchpad for serious American drama.
Its greatest early voice was Eugene O'Neill, born right here at the long-gone Barrett Hotel, 1500 Broadway.
He debuted many of his plays on these stages, including the Pulitzer winners Beyond the Horizon and Anna Christie.
Then, in 1943, Broadway landed its first runaway hit — Oklahoma!, which ran a record 2,212 performances.
O'Neill's success cleared the way for Tennessee Williams, Arthur Miller and Edward Albee, a legacy the Tony Awards began honoring in 1947.
Today those shows play in one of 41 official Broadway theaters, lavish early-20th-century jewels ringing the square.
The whole scene got its own portrait in the 2014 Oscar-winner Birdman.
A washed-up Michael Keaton is trying to stage a Broadway adaptation at the St James Theatre on West 44th, gets locked out, and ends up marching through Times Square in nothing but his underwear.
A few blocks east, he spars over the play with Lindsay Duncan at the historic drinking den Rum House.
And that brings our walk to a close.
Thank you for coming along with me today — when you're ready, take your time and keep exploring on your own.
